replacement: Here Ippolit Kirillovitch turned to a detailed account of all Mitya’s attempts to borrow the money. He described the visit to Samsonov and the journey to Lyagavy. “Harassed, jeered at, hungry, he had sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him, a likely story). He was tortured by jealousy at having left the object of his affections behind in the town, and he suspected she would go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away. At last he came back to the town, and to his joy found that she had not gone near his father. He took her himself to her protector. (Strange to say, he does not seem to have been jealous of Samsonov, which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his ambush in the back gardens, and there he learns that Smerdyakov is in a fit and the other servant is ill. The coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals.’ What a temptation! Still he resists it. He goes to see a lady who has lived in our town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady had long followed his career with compassion. She gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, and the waste of his youth and strength in pot-house debauchery, and to set off for the gold mines of Siberia. ‘That would be an outlet for your turbulent energy, your romantic character, your thirst for adventure.’”
